title: TCS Just Handed 50,000 Employees an AI Co-Worker. India's IT Industry Is Bracing for What Comes Next.
excerpt: The Anthropic deal is the biggest enterprise AI deployment by an Indian company — and the clearest signal yet that the $315 billion IT services model is being rebuilt from the inside.
body:
Tata Consultancy Services, India's largest IT exporter, has struck a global partnership with Anthropic that will put the American AI company's Claude models in the hands of 50,000 TCS employees across engineering, finance, legal, marketing, and sales. A new dedicated business unit will build customer-facing AI solutions on top of Claude.

The deal, announced on June 11 as a stock exchange filing, makes TCS a Global Premier Partner in the Claude Partner Network — and the partnership's scale dwarfs anything India's IT industry has attempted before with frontier AI.

## What the Deal Looks Like

TCS will get early access to Anthropic's newest Claude models and use that head start to develop industry-specific AI solutions for clients in financial services, healthcare, aviation, telecom, and public services. The company's U.K.-based life-and-pensions subsidiary Diligenta, which serves over 22 million customers, will deploy Claude for customer service and process automation. TCS iON, its digital learning platform, will offer training and certification on Anthropic's models.

The internal deployment of Claude to 50,000 employees is not altruism — it is a laboratory. TCS intends to use its own workforce as a testing ground, generating the kind of operational data that can then be packaged and sold to enterprise clients pursuing their own AI transformations.

"Enterprise AI value comes from understanding business context, orchestrating complex systems, and applying deep AI engineering talent," TCS CEO K. Krithivasan said.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called the partnership a deepening of the company's commitment to India, which he described as Anthropic's second-largest market.

## The Industry Is Already Shrinking

The partnership arrives against a backdrop of existential anxiety for India's IT services sector. TCS and Infosys shares have fallen roughly 34 and 31 per cent this year, respectively. The Nifty IT index has dropped 27 per cent in 2026 alone — not a cyclical pullback, analysts say, but a structural repricing of the entire outsourcing model.

TCS Chairman N. Chandrasekaran said at the company's annual general meeting that TCS is moving toward having "an equal number of employees and AI agents" in its workforce. Last July, the company cut more than 12,000 jobs. Headcount fell by over 23,000 on a net basis in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

Infosys struck a similar partnership with Anthropic in February. OpenAI has roped in both Infosys and HCLTech for comparable arrangements. The pattern is unmistakable: India's IT giants are not just adopting AI tools — they are rebuilding their business models around them.

## The Anthropic Connection Gets Complicated

The timing of the TCS deal is layered with irony. Just days earlier, the U.S. government ordered Anthropic to disable its most powerful AI models — Fable 5 and Mythos — for users who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents, citing national security and export controls. The move sent a chill through India's tech community.

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu urged Indian organisations to embrace open-source and Chinese AI models instead. "Technology is the ultimate weapon," he wrote on X. Former Infosys executive Mohandas Pai went further, calling on the Indian government to create an annual ₹500 billion ($5 billion) fund for AI and deep tech, alongside a ₹2 trillion credit guarantee for infrastructure.

The tension is clear: Indian IT firms are building their futures on American AI platforms, even as American policy is drawing new lines around who gets to use the most advanced versions of those platforms.

## What It Means for NRI Tech Workers

For the roughly 1.5 million Indians employed by TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and their peers — many of them on H-1B visas in the United States — the partnership is both threat and lifeline. The threat: AI agents that can write code, draft contracts, and analyse financial data will reduce the need for human headcount. The lifeline: employees who learn to work alongside Claude, and who can deploy it for clients, become more valuable, not less.

The broader question is whether India's IT services sector can make this transition fast enough to avoid the kind of hollowing-out that hit American manufacturing. The industry generates $315 billion in annual revenue and employs millions directly and indirectly. If the AI pivot works, it becomes the world's largest laboratory for human-AI collaboration. If it does not, the consequences ripple from Bengaluru to the Bay Area.

*Sources: Reuters, TechCrunch, The Hindu BusinessLine, Outlook Business, Trade Brains*
